Oakvale Food Cooperative — A Community-Owned Grocery

Welcome! This page is for anyone thinking about shopping with us as a member. Below you will find how our cooperative works and the simple steps to join.

How our co-op works

Oakvale is owned by the people who shop here. Since we opened in 2009, our members have shared in the decisions that shape the store, from the products we stock to the local farms we partner with. Members are not employees; they are neighbors who help guide the store and buy their weekly groceries here. Today more than 1,200 households hold a membership. Two years ago, members funded a new solar roof, which now supplies part of our electricity. All members also receive a monthly newsletter and reduced prices on cooking workshops.

A shared goal this year

This year we are working to open a fresh bakery counter at the back of the store. Building it is a demanding project that cannot be finished by staff alone. It will require both contributions from members and hours of volunteer help. We expect the counter to open before the end of the year, offering bread baked on site each morning.

Becoming a member

Joining is easy. First, complete a short form at the customer service desk. Second, pay a one-time equity share of $25, which is refunded if you ever decide to leave. Third, attend a brief orientation so you understand how the store runs. There is no monthly charge, and your share makes you a part-owner right away.

Store hours: Monday to Saturday, 8:00 A.M. to 8:00 P.M. Questions? Speak with any staff member or stop by the service desk. We look forward to welcoming you.

questionGroups.title: Questions 181-185
questionGroups.passageHtml:
Workshop Spotlight

Cut, Stitch, Repeat

By Rebecca Lyle

A quiet studio in Braxton is teaching newcomers to make their own leather goods entirely by hand.

On a side street in Braxton, behind the wide windows of Thornbury Leather Studio, a row of visitors bend over their workbenches, pressing needles through strips of tan hide. None of them had made anything from leather before this month, and that is exactly the point. This spring the studio began offering a set of hands-on workshops built for complete beginners, and the seats have been filling quickly.

The program is arranged in three levels. First Stitch, the entry point, is a single two-hour session that requires no experience and sends participants home with a finished card holder. Everyday Carry runs across two evenings and guides makers through cutting, dyeing, and assembling a folded wallet. The longest option, Satchel Studio, fills a full weekend and ends with a completed shoulder bag. Each level draws a different sort of visitor, from the curious first-timer to the hobbyist ready for a larger project. Tools and materials are provided at every level.

Every session is led in person by Julian Reyes, who opened the studio after spending three years apprenticing with a saddlemaker in Florence. "I was taught slowly, by hand, and that is how I teach here," Reyes said. "People are surprised by how much they can finish in one sitting once someone shows them where to place the needle."

Classes run on weekday evenings and weekends, and places can be reserved through the studio's website. Reyes recommends First Stitch as a starting point for anyone unsure whether the craft suits them.

----------------------

Rating: 5 out of 5 stars
Workshop attended: First Stitch
Would recommend: Yes
Review title: Made something real in one afternoon
Posted by: newtocraft_gina
Date: May 14

I booked the shortest class on the list because I only wanted to find out whether making things by hand was for me, and I had never picked up a leather tool in my life. Two hours later I walked out with a card holder that I had cut and stitched myself. The person leading the session was endlessly patient. At one point he mentioned that he had been shaping and repairing leather since he was a boy, and it showed in the way he fixed our mistakes without ever taking the work out of our hands. The studio sits inside an old glove factory just a few streets from my apartment, one I had walked past for years without going in. I am already looking at signing up for the wallet class next.

A Fresh Look for Ashcombe Kitchen and Table

By Damien Cross, Westport

When Ashcombe Kitchen and Table opened its newest branch in Westport last month, shoppers found more than the cookware and tableware the company has built its name on.

The retailer, which has run its established stores in Redmill for more than a decade, picked Westport for its latest expansion and is said to be weighing a further store in Northgate.

Owner Marguerite Vance credited the store's bright new look partly to its flooring. Contractors laid durable vinyl plank across roughly 200 square meters of sales floor, leveled the subfloor beneath it, and finished every edge with matching trim — all completed in four working days.

"The floor makes the whole space feel finished," Vance said. "Customers notice it the moment they walk in."
